HEADER.TITLE: Starting your studies in Australia
HEADER.SUBTITLE: A practical reference for arriving, enrolling, and settling in — from the week before you land to your first exam period. Bookmark this page; you won't need all of it on day one.

CH01.TITLE: Six weeks out: what to lock in first
CH01.CHECK1: Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE) issued by your institution — everything else, including your visa, is built on this.
CH01.CHECK2: Student visa (subclass 500) granted, with your visa grant letter saved as PDF and printed.
CH01.CHECK3: Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) purchased for your full visa duration — it's a visa condition, not optional.
CH01.CHECK4: Accommodation booked for at least your first 2–4 weeks so you're not house-hunting jet-lagged.
CH01.CHECK5: Flights booked to arrive a few days before orientation, not the night before.
CH01.CHECK6: Scans of your passport, visa grant, CoE, OSHC certificate, and transcripts saved to cloud storage, separate from your luggage.
CH01.NOTE: Seasons are reversed. December–February is summer, June–August is winter. A Semester 1 start (February) means arriving in late-summer heat; a Semester 2 start (July) means arriving in winter — pack accordingly.
CH01.LUGGAGE1: Passport, visa grant letter, CoE, and OSHC certificate
CH01.LUGGAGE2: Proof of accommodation for your first nights
CH01.LUGGAGE3: A small amount of Australian dollars for transport and food on arrival
CH01.LUGGAGE4: Prescription medication, in original packaging with your name on it

CH02.TITLE: The admin chain: do these in order
CH02.INTRO: A bank account needs an address, a phone plan often needs a bank card, and paid work needs a tax number — each step unlocks the next.
CH02.ROW1_WHY: Finalises enrolment, campus tour, ID card, support services
CH02.ROW2_WHY: Needed for library, labs, printing, transport concessions
CH02.ROW3_WHY: Get paid if you work; pay rent and bills without cash
CH02.ROW3_NEED: Passport, visa, enrolment letter, local address
CH02.ROW4_TASK: Apply for a Tax File Number
CH02.ROW4_WHY: Required before starting any paid job — free via the ATO
CH02.ROW5_WHY: Links Medicare/OSHC, tax, and (if eligible) Centrelink
CH02.ROW6_WHY: Confirms you can claim doctor visits from day one
CH02.TIP: Some banks let you open an account online before you land — CommBank, NAB, and ANZ all offer this to international students with a CoE, so you're not carrying cash for two weeks.

CH03.TITLE: Know your census date
CH03.CARD1_ITEM3: A mid-year and end-of-year break of several weeks
CH03.CARD1_ITEM4: Some courses run trimesters instead — check your own calendar
CH03.CARD2_ITEM2: A census date, usually ~3–4 weeks in
CH03.CARD2_ITEM4: A formal exam or assessment period at the end
CH03.WARN: The census date is the most important date each semester. Withdraw before it and there's no financial or academic penalty. Withdraw after, and you're generally still billed, and it can appear as a fail. Put every census date in your calendar the day enrolment opens.
CH03.ENROL1: Check your course structure — core vs elective units, prerequisites — in your course handbook.
CH03.ENROL2: Enrol via the student portal before the deadline.
CH03.ENROL3: Confirm your study load meets your visa's full-time requirement.
CH03.ENROL4: Check your timetable for clashes before census.

CH04.TITLE: What's different from many overseas systems
CH04.ITEM1: Lectures and tutorials are separate — the tutorial or lab is small, discussion-based, and usually where attendance is actually tracked.
CH04.ITEM2: Assessment is continuous, not one final exam — expect essays, quizzes, presentations, and group work across the semester.
CH04.ITEM3: Academic integrity is enforced strictly, including on AI-generated text. When in doubt, cite it.
CH04.ITEM4: Grades typically run High Distinction / Distinction / Credit / Pass / Fail — exact bands vary by institution.
CH04.ITEM5: Emailing academic staff is normal — most list consultation hours and reply within a few working days.

CH05.TITLE: Settling into a multicultural country
CH05.INTRO: Roughly a third of Australia's residents were born overseas. You will not be the only international student, and you won't be far from food, faith communities, or language from home.
CH05.QUOTE: Before European settlement, this land was cared for by hundreds of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations, whose connection to it spans over 60,000 years. You'll hear an "Acknowledgement of Country" at orientation, graduations, and public events — a normal, respectful part of Australian civic life.
CH05.ITEM1: Directness reads as normal, not rude — first names are used quickly, including with lecturers.
CH05.ITEM2: Tipping isn't expected — hospitality staff earn a legal minimum wage.
CH05.ITEM3: Punctuality matters for class; social plans are looser.
CH05.ITEM4: Queuing is taken seriously — wait your turn.
CH05.ITEM5: Public conversation is kept low-key, especially on transport.

CH06.TITLE: Budgeting week to week
CH06.INTRO: Costs vary sharply by city — Sydney and Melbourne run highest, regional campuses noticeably cheaper. Broad weekly ranges for a student sharing accommodation, in AUD:
CH06.ROW1_NOTES: Higher in inner-city Sydney/Melbourne; lower regionally
CH06.ROW2_NOTES: Cooking at home is far cheaper than eating out
CH06.ROW3_NOTES: Concession fares reduce this where eligible
CH06.WARN: Never wire money, share your banking password, or send a rental deposit before inspecting in person or by video call. Rental and job scams specifically target new arrivals in their first weeks.

CH07.TITLE: On-campus vs share housing
CH07.CARD1_ITEM1: Simplest option for your first semester — no lease, bills usually included
CH07.CARD1_ITEM2: Built-in social community, closest to classes
CH07.CARD1_ITEM3: Apply early; popular colleges fill months ahead
CH07.CARD2_ITEM1: Cheaper long-term; listed on realestate.com.au, domain.com.au, flatmates.com.au
CH07.CARD2_ITEM2: Requires a lease and a bond (typically 4 weeks' rent, held by a government bond authority)
CH07.CARD2_ITEM3: Inspect in person or via live video call before paying anything
CH07.TIP: Book temporary accommodation for your first two to four weeks rather than signing a 12-month lease sight-unseen. It gives you time to inspect share houses in person once you know your timetable.

CH08.TITLE: Get your smart card in week one
CH08.NOTE: Concession fares aren't automatic for international students — eligibility differs by state and sometimes visa subclass. Ask your international student office which concession, if any, applies to you.
CH08.INTRO: Australia drives on the left. You can generally drive on a valid overseas licence for a limited period after arrival — the exact window is set by your state's road authority.

CH09.TITLE: Know your visa's work-hour limit
CH09.WARN: Subclass 500 work rights are currently capped at 48 hours per fortnight while your course is in session, uncapped during official breaks. These rules change periodically — confirm the current limit with the Department of Home Affairs or your institution before starting any job.
CH09.ITEM1: Get your Tax File Number ready — without one, tax is withheld at the top rate.
CH09.ITEM2: Confirm you'll be paid at least the national minimum wage, with payslips.
CH09.ITEM3: Check you're being paid superannuation if eligible.
CH09.ITEM4: The Fair Work Ombudsman investigates underpayment for free and confidentially, regardless of visa status.

CH10.TITLE: Cover, sun, and emergencies
CH10.ITEM1: OSHC is your primary cover for the length of your visa and is compulsory.
CH10.ITEM2: Some nationalities have a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement with Australia — check if yours applies.
CH10.ITEM3: Book a GP for non-urgent issues; save emergency departments for genuine emergencies.
CH10.TIP: Australia has some of the world's highest UV levels, even on mild days. Slip on a shirt, slop on SPF 30+, slap on a hat, seek shade, slide on sunglasses.

CH11.TITLE: Use your support services early
CH11.ITEM1: International student advisors — visa conditions, OSHC claims, general welfare.
CH11.ITEM2: Student union / guild — free advocacy for academic and tenancy disputes.
CH11.ITEM3: Counselling services — confidential, usually free for a set number of sessions.
CH11.ITEM4: Study Australia and the Department of Home Affairs websites are the authoritative sources for visa condition changes.

CH12.TITLE: Slang you'll hear in week one
CH12.ROW4_MEANS: A greeting, not a real question
CH12.ROW7_MEANS: Bring a dish to share at a gathering

PLAN_AHEAD.TITLE: The decisions that are hard to undo later
PLAN_AHEAD.SUBTITLE: General guidance drawn from students and staff who've been through this before. This is general information only, not migration advice — for guidance specific to your situation, book a consultation with a registered migration agent.
PLAN_AHEAD.NOTE_BODY: We wrote this page because we've sat across the table from too many students — and parents — who found out about a deadline, a document, or a visa rule only after it was too late to do anything about it. Almost everything below could have changed the outcome if someone had known it six months earlier.
PLAN_AHEAD.INTRO_BODY: Visa and course decisions are usually easiest to get right the first time. Once you're partway through a course, or a visa application is already lodged, some changes become slow, expensive, or no longer possible at all — so the earlier you plan, the more options you keep open.
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE1_TITLE: Choose your course with your visa goal in mind
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE1_BODY: If skilled migration is part of your plan, your course choice matters more than it used to. Migration law changes frequently, and switching to a different course partway through your studies is generally far more restricted than it once was. Research which qualifications align with your migration pathway before you enrol — it's much easier to choose carefully now than to change course later.
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE_APPLY_LABEL: When you apply for your visa
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE_APPLY_TITLE: Answer the Genuine Student questions specifically
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE_APPLY_BODY: Since March 2024, student visa applications are assessed against the Genuine Student requirement rather than the older Genuine Temporary Entrant test. You'll be asked targeted questions about your study plans, ties to home, and career goals. Vague or copy-pasted answers are one of the most common reasons applications are delayed or refused, so take the time to answer specifically and honestly.
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE_CONDITIONS_TITLE: Know the conditions attached to your visa
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE_CONDITIONS_BODY: A student visa comes with conditions, not just a start and end date. You're generally required to maintain satisfactory course attendance and progress — commonly interpreted as passing at least half your units each study period — and there's usually a cap on how many hours you can work while classes are in session (currently 48 hours per fortnight, unlimited during official breaks; rules and figures do change, so confirm the current settings). Breaching a condition isn't just paperwork — it can put the visa itself at risk.
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE2_LABEL: If you need to travel mid-course
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE2_TITLE: Travelling while on a Bridging Visa A
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE2_BODY: If you're on a Bridging Visa A and plan to travel outside Australia, you will generally need to apply for a Bridging Visa B before you leave. Without one, you may not be able to legally return. Speak with a registered migration agent well before you book any travel.
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE3_TITLE: Start preparing for your next visa early
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE3_BODY: If a Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) is next for you, start gathering documents around six months before you graduate rather than after. That gives you time to re-sit an English test if a result has expired, and to request documents that can take weeks to arrive.
PLAN_AHEAD.DOC1: Graduation certificate (or a completion letter while you wait for it)
PLAN_AHEAD.DOC3: A valid English test result (e.g. IELTS) — results are generally only valid for a limited time, so check before you rely on an old one
PLAN_AHEAD.STAGE3_CALLOUT: If the subclass 485 is part of your plan, check the current age limit well before your final year — it has been lowered for most applicants in recent years — and confirm exactly how long your English test result stays valid, since sitting it again close to your deadline adds pressure you don't need.
PLAN_AHEAD.CLOSING_BODY_STRONG: Choosing right at the very start is almost always far cheaper and far easier than trying to fix it later.
PLAN_AHEAD.CLOSING_BODY_REST: Every situation is straightforward to handle before you're in the middle of it. Once you're partway through a course or a visa application, changing direction is often still possible — but it's rarely quick, rarely cheap, and the delay can affect years of your life: a postponed graduation, lost work rights, or a migration pathway that's no longer open to you.
PLAN_AHEAD.CLOSING_485_STRONG: The Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485) doesn't last as long as most students expect.
PLAN_AHEAD.CLOSING_485_REST: How deliberately you use that window — building relevant work experience, tracking points-test criteria, keeping your next visa in mind — can make a real difference to what's still possible once it ends. Start planning for it well before it's running out, not after.
PLAN_AHEAD.CLOSING_TAGLINE: Always plan ahead — before it's too late.
PLAN_AHEAD.FINAL_LINE: It doesn't have to be us. A QEAC-certified education counsellor can help with course and study decisions; anything visa or migration related needs a registered migration agent. Just ask someone — while you still have time to act on the answer.
